title: US-Iran Ceasefire Collapses at Halfway Mark as Strikes Intensify and Hormuz Crisis Deepens
excerpt: Thirty days into the 60-day negotiating window, the memorandum of understanding has unravelled into escalating attacks, threatening global energy markets and India's oil supply chain.
body:
• The June 17 US-Iran memorandum of understanding has collapsed less than a month after signing, with Trump declaring the ceasefire "over" after Iranian attacks on commercial shipping
  • The US has conducted six consecutive days of airstrikes on Iranian military targets, while Iran has retaliated by hitting American bases in Kuwait, Jordan, Bahrain, and Qatar
  • The Strait of Hormuz — through which roughly 20 percent of global oil passes — remains contested, with Iran insisting on controlling vessel passage and charging transit fees
  • The crisis directly threatens India's energy security, as approximately 60 percent of its crude oil imports transit through the strait

How the Deal Fell Apart

https://x.com/Chris_1791/status/2078167684793938066

The memorandum of understanding signed on June 17 in Islamabad was supposed to deliver three things: an immediate halt to military operations, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and a 60-day window for negotiations on Iran's nuclear programme and regional security. Thirty days in, all three objectives are in ruins.

The unravelling began when Iran attacked three commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz around July 6-7, violating the MOU's prohibition on interference with commercial shipping. The US responded with strikes on Iranian territory on July 8. Trump declared the ceasefire "over," and the administration withdrew one of its most significant concessions — a temporary waiver allowing Iran to sell oil — and restored the naval blockade that had been lifted after the agreement was signed.

Six Days of Escalating Strikes

Since the ceasefire collapsed, the US has launched strikes on Iranian military targets for six consecutive days. Targets have included coastal installations along the Strait of Hormuz, road bridges, and an oil tanker at Kharg Island — Iran's main oil export terminal. Separate reports indicate attacks near Bushehr, which houses Iran's only nuclear power plant.

Iran has struck back at American bases in Kuwait, Jordan, Bahrain, and Qatar — the four Arab countries hosting US forces in the region. In Kuwait, strikes hit a water desalination and electricity plant. Iran also targeted a Jordanian air base that Washington had upgraded into a regional headquarters, claiming it was the launch site for a strike near a children's cancer hospital in Ahvaz.

"The warring sides are back to square one, reaching the limits of what they can achieve in the context of limited war and will eventually face a choice of whether to back down or escalate."

— Alex Vatanka, Director of the Iran Program, Middle East Institute

The Hormuz Question

At the heart of the crisis is control over the Strait of Hormuz. Iran wants all vessels to use a channel close to its shores and intends to charge passage fees. Washington has encouraged ships to use an alternative route along the Omani coast. Iranian military spokesperson Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia said US airstrikes could never break Iran's grip on the strait because Iran can target it from anywhere on its territory.

The White House said the strait is open for ships not travelling to or from Iranian ports, with the US Navy ensuring passage. But the contested status of the waterway — through which roughly 20 percent of the world's oil supply passes — has already triggered a systemic crisis in global energy markets. Gold dropped below $4,000 and bond yields are signalling potential Fed rate hikes as inflation fears mount.

What This Means for India

India is among the most exposed nations. Approximately 60 percent of the country's crude oil imports transit through the Strait of Hormuz, making any disruption a direct threat to energy security and the broader economy. The Indian Navy has already deployed vessels to protect its interests in the region, and the government has been scrambling to diversify supply routes.

The crisis also complicates India's diplomatic balancing act. New Delhi maintains relationships with both Washington and Tehran, and has historically benefited from Iranian oil imports. The US sanctions bill that could impose 100 percent tariffs on India over Russian oil purchases adds another layer of pressure on Indian policymakers navigating an increasingly volatile global energy landscape.

With 30 days remaining in the negotiating window, the White House insists Iran has made a "fresh overture" to resume talks. Whether that translates into substantive diplomacy or merely delays a deeper escalation remains the defining question of this crisis.
